turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Number 149! Good heavens! It appears we are delving into a veritable abyss of social obscurity. Tell me, Mr. Worthing, does this Lady Bloxham, in her advanced years, possess a lineage of impeccable standing?

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Indeed, Lady Bracknell. I believe her family has been established in the county for… for quite some time. I’m afraid the precise details of their lineage escape me at present, but I’m certain they are… perfectly respectable.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: “Perfectly respectable is hardly a superlative, Mr. Worthing. One expects a degree of *distinction*, wouldn't you agree? It is scarcely sufficient to merely *exist* within a respectable family; one must actively *contribute* to its reputation.”,

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Mother, really! Must you interrogate the poor man so? Mr. Worthing is *perfectly* suitable, and I have already declared my engagement, as you are well aware.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Gwendolen, my dear, your declarations are charmingly impetuous, but they do not absolve me from the responsibility of ensuring a suitable match. An engagement, you see, is a serious undertaking, not a trifle to be bandied about with the casualness of a misplaced glove. We must proceed with due diligence, Mr. Worthing, and I have many more questions for you.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I… I quite understand, Lady Bracknell. I certainly wouldn't wish to rush into anything without proper consideration. Perhaps, if you’d permit, I could consult my… my memory on the particulars of Lady Bloxham's family history?

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Consulting one's memory, Mr. Worthing, is a commendable habit, though I suspect it will prove a rather fruitless exercise in this instance. Let us dispense with the pretense of familial knowledge and proceed to matters of *genuine* importance: your profession, your income, and, most crucially, your parentage.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: My… my profession, Lady Bracknell? I am, er, a gentleman of leisure, you see. As for income, I have… sufficient means to provide comfortably, I assure you.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: A gentleman of leisure! How delightfully vague, Mr. Worthing. One trusts your leisure is not spent in pursuits unbecoming of a man who aspires to associate with my family, for idle hands, as the saying goes, are the devil's playthings.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Indeed, Lady Bracknell. I assure you, my leisure is devoted to… to pursuits of a decidedly respectable nature! I find great enjoyment in country walks, charitable works, and the occasional game of rackets, all of which, I believe, are quite in keeping with a gentleman’s proper activities.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Rackets, Mr. Worthing? A most unsuitable pastime, I must say. It encourages an unseemly display of physical exertion, and I shudder to think what sort of impression it might give to one's acquaintances. Pray, elaborate on these 'charitable works' - I trust they do not involve associating with the lower orders?

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: My charitable works, Lady Bracknell, are primarily focused on assisting those… those in need within the local community. I endeavour to provide quietly, you see, without drawing undue attention to myself or the recipients. I would hardly wish to cause any… discomfort, naturally.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Quietly, you say? Mr. Worthing, discretion is a virtue, certainly, but a man of your prospects should also demonstrate a certain… *public* commitment to the betterment of society. One cannot simply disappear into the shadows, you know. Tell me, are these recipients of your charity aware of your generous contributions?

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Of course, Lady Bracknell. While I do prefer to maintain a degree of… privacy regarding my charitable endeavors, I believe some awareness amongst those who benefit is, naturally, desirable. It's important that they feel… supported, wouldn't you agree?

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Supported, Mr. Worthing? A most curious sentiment! It suggests a lack of understanding of the delicate balance between generosity and presumption. I daresay, the truly grateful recipient requires no explicit acknowledgement of his benefactor’s kindness.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Mother, really! Mr. Worthing is being perfectly agreeable, and you’re subjecting him to the most dreadful inquisition. Surely, a gentleman of his obvious charm and… *potential*… deserves a little more consideration?

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Charm, my dear Gwendolen, is a superficial quality, easily mistaken for substance. Mr. Worthing’s adherence to ‘privacy’ regarding his philanthropic endeavors is… unsettling, to say the least. One wonders what he is attempting to conceal.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I assure you, Lady Bracknell, there's absolutely nothing I'm attempting to conceal! It's merely that I find the publicity surrounding such matters… rather distracting from the actual work being done. I simply wish to avoid any undue attention being drawn away from those in need.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Distracting, Mr. Worthing? It appears you possess a rather novel interpretation of philanthropy. One would think a gentleman of your apparent resources would welcome the opportunity to demonstrate his virtue to the world, rather than shy away from it.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Indeed, Lady Bracknell. I do believe in demonstrating virtue through action, rather than pronouncements. Perhaps I’ve not been entirely clear – it is the *expectation* of praise that I find uncomfortable, not the act of giving itself.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: I am engaged to Mr. Worthing, mamma.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Pardon me, you are not engaged to any one. When you do become engaged to some one, I, or your father, should his health permit him, will inform you of the fact. An engagement should come on a young girl as a surprise, pleasant or unpleasant, as the case may be. It is hardly a matter that she could be allowed to arrange for herself . . . And now I have a few questions to put to you, Mr. Worthing. While I am making these inquiries, you, Gwendolen, will wait for me below in the carriage.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Mamma!

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: In the carriage, Gwendolen!

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Gwendolen, the carriage!

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Yes, mamma.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: You can take a seat, Mr. Worthing.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Thank you, Lady Bracknell, I prefer standing.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I feel bound to tell you that you are not down on my list of eligible young men, although I have the same list as the dear Duchess of Bolton has. We work together, in fact. However, I am quite ready to enter your name, should your answers be what a really affectionate mother requires. Do you smoke?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Well, yes, I must admit I smoke.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I am glad to hear it. A man should always have an occupation of some kind. There are far too many idle men in London as it is. How old are you?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Twenty-nine.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: A very good age to be married at. I have always been of opinion that a man who desires to get married should know either everything or nothing. Which do you know?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: I know nothing, Lady Bracknell.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I am pleased to hear it. I do not approve of anything that tampers with natural ignorance. Ignorance is like a delicate exotic fruit; touch it and the bloom is gone. The whole theory of modern education is radically unsound. Fortunately in England, at any rate, education produces no effect whatsoever. If it did, it would prove a serious danger to the upper classes, and probably lead to acts of violence in Grosvenor Square. What is your income?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Between seven and eight thousand a year.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: In land, or in investments?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: In investments, chiefly.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: What between the duties expected of one during one’s lifetime, and the duties exacted from one after one’s death, land has ceased to be either a profit or a pleasure. It gives one position, and prevents one from keeping it up. That’s all that can be said about land.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: I have a country house with some land, of course, attached to it, about fifteen hundred acres, I believe; but I don’t depend on that for my real income. In fact, as far as I can make out, the poachers are the only people who make anything out of it.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: A country house! How many bedrooms? Well, that point can be cleared up afterwards. You have a town house, I hope? A girl with a simple, unspoiled nature, like Gwendolen, could hardly be expected to reside in the country.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Well, I own a house in Belgrave Square, but it is let by the year to Lady Bloxham. Of course, I can get it back whenever I like, at six months’ notice.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bloxham? I don’t know her.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Oh, she goes about very little. She is a lady considerably advanced in years.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Ah, nowadays that is no guarantee of respectability of character. What number in Belgrave Square?
